title: Application Availability and Resilience
learning_outcomes: Explain the main security concern and trust boundary involved in Application Availability and Resilience.
Choose an appropriate defensive control for Application Availability and Resilience and state the assumptions under which it works.
Define a safe, reproducible verification step for Application Availability and Resilience, including a relevant negative or failure case.

content.intro: This lesson belongs to Module 18: Security Configuration, Infrastructure, and Deployment Architecture. It builds practical understanding of Application Availability and Resilience with the syllabus subtopics retained below.
content.why_it_matters: Application Availability and Resilience makes secure behavior repeatable across implementation, dependencies, configuration, and release. Enforce business invariants on the server inside atomic transactions or with database constraints, and test duplicates, retries, concurrency, and invalid state transitions.

content_blocks.title: The core idea
content_blocks.text: Application Availability and Resilience can be understood through this sequence: Define requirement → Implement least privilege → Automate verification → Review exceptions. Start with the application asset and trust boundary, state what secure behavior should occur, and identify the evidence that would prove or disprove it.

content_blocks.title: Connect the syllabus subtopics
content_blocks.text: The source curriculum groups this lesson around: 138.1 Timeouts and bounded resource consumption; 138.2 Request and concurrency limits; 138.3 Retry storms and cascading failures; 138.4 Graceful degradation; 138.5 Backups and recovery procedures; 138.6 Security and availability trade-offs. Treat these points as a checklist, not a list to memorize: explain the risk, identify the root cause, select a control, and define a test for that control.

items.title: Scope
items.text: Identify the asset, principal, input, state, or boundary affected. State whether the example is local, owned, or explicitly authorized.

items.title: Control
items.text: Enforce business invariants on the server inside atomic transactions or with database constraints, and test duplicates, retries, concurrency, and invalid state transitions.

items.title: Failure behavior
items.text: Include an invalid, denied, expired, malformed, repeated, or otherwise relevant boundary case. Fail safely without exposing secrets.

items.title: Evidence
items.text: Record expected versus actual behavior, a sanitized request or test result, the root cause, the chosen fix, and the regression test.

content_blocks.expected_output: The policy describes example caps for request size, timeout, per-user traffic, and expensive-operation concurrency.
content_blocks.run_instructions: These are demonstration values, not universal recommendations. Tune limits to measured workload and enforce them server-side across instances.
content_blocks.reset_steps: Use a clean local test account and synthetic data. Reset the test fixture after recording the result; do not include credentials or private data in the course report.

content_blocks.title: Common mistake and recovery
content_blocks.text: Do not confuse an observation with proof or rely on a UI-only restriction. Enforce business invariants on the server inside atomic transactions or with database constraints, and test duplicates, retries, concurrency, and invalid state transitions. If evidence is ambiguous, reduce the test to one condition, inspect the application code/configuration, and repeat only within the permitted scope.

content_blocks.title: Execution and safety boundary
content_blocks.text: The current CodeLeaf playground is an HTML/CSS/JavaScript preview, not a secure runner for arbitrary server code. This example is a static reference unless the run instructions explicitly identify a supported local environment. Use a private local lab or a test system with written authorization; do not test unrelated public systems.

content.task: For “Application Availability and Resilience”, write a short security note or test in a local/owned application. Identify the expected secure behavior, at least one relevant failure case, and the evidence needed to prove the control works.
task_acceptance_criteria: Explain the core rule for Application Availability and Resilience in your own words.
Name the trust boundary and the server-side control or policy that applies.
Specify a repeatable test for expected behavior and a relevant denied/failure path.
Use synthetic data and redact credentials, tokens, and personal information from evidence.
hints: Start by stating the asset, input, actor, or trust boundary and the expected secure behavior.
Change one condition at a time; record expected and actual outcomes with synthetic data.
Check the linked official reference for framework-specific settings and version-dependent behavior.
content.expected_output: A concise control explanation and a sanitized test record showing expected/actual behavior, one failure case, and a regression check.
recap: Application Availability and Resilience is a security boundary/control topic, not a standalone checklist item.
Enforce business invariants on the server inside atomic transactions or with database constraints, and test duplicates, retries, concurrency, and invalid state transitions.
Retest fixes and record sanitized evidence; use only authorized environments.
